This message comes from Odoo, the all-in-one business management software platform.
Whether you're a small or large business, Odoo gives you one flexible platform built to grow with you.
Try today for free at Odoo.com/NPRPodcasts.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Both the U.S. and China say they're reducing tariff rates on a small fraction of goods they trade.
The two countries have been negotiating on these reductions for months.
It's one of the few concrete outcomes from China's state visit to Washington this week, as NPR's Emily Fang reports.
After Trump visited Beijing in May, the two countries have been working to find $30 billion of non-sensitive goods each to reduce tariffs on.
But that's a small slice of the more than $400 billion volume of U.S.-China annual trade.
And two ongoing trade investigations into China on potentially unfair trading practices will likely raise overall U.S. tariff rates on China again in the coming weeks.
Following Xi's visit to the U.S., the two countries have also agreed to start an A.I. dialogue starting in November.
The U.S. and China held high-level A.I. dialogues during the Biden administration, where both Biden and Xi Jinping agreed A.I. should remain under human control.
Xi repeated the need for humans to control A.I. in its opening remarks while visiting Washington on Thursday.
Emily Fang and Pure News, Washington.
The White House barred CNN from accompanying President Trump on his trip to watch a college football game in Tennessee earlier today.
The network was scheduled to provide TV pool coverage of that trip.
This comes just hours after the Trump administration restored access for the network's journalists to the White House, along with Politico and MS Now.
And Pure's David Folkinflict has more.
Right now, all of the other members of the pool are refusing to step in.
So CNN is joined by CBS, ABC, NBC and Fox News.
So those guys are all stepping away.
So what you have instead are kind of these other outfits which are not part of the pool and are essentially aligned with the president.
You have RAV, which is Real America's voice, manning this flight to Tennessee today.
And in town, you have Lindell TV.
That's named for Mike Lindell, the My Pillow Guy.
And Pure's David Folkinflict reporting.
A powerful nor'easter is slamming the Northeast, prompting states of emergency to be declared in parts of New York and New Jersey, where flooding's already taking place.
Steve Castenbaum reports more than 31 million people are under coastal flood warnings and advisories from the Carolinas up through New England.
With wind gusts between 40 and 60 miles per hour, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said the impact of the storm would be felt most along the coast.
Lots of coastal flooding, perhaps even some erosion that could lead to downed trees, and that means downed power lines.
A foot or two of water covered low-lying coastal areas of New York during high tide.
The storm was pushing water up into several New Jersey shore towns.
Streets in Surf City looked more like canals.
In Delaware, the storm surge pushed an ocean buoy up into Rehoboth Beach.
The effects of this nor'easter are expected to last until Monday.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Castenbaum in New York.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and TikTok are refusing to run advertisements for an upcoming documentary on billionaire Elon Musk.
As NPR's Bobby Allen reports, Musk has threatened to sue over the nearly four-hour film, which he calls a "hit job."
The documentary is called Musk, it's by Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney, and it's set for release next month.
The film is a scathing look at the tech mogul's life from his childhood in South Africa, his rise in Silicon Valley,
including his takeover of the site formerly known as Twitter, along with his time in the White House.
Gibney asks, "How did one man become so powerful?"
It's a message deemed too political by meta, YouTube and TikTok, all of which have refused to carry ads about the film.
That's according to a person close to the production who wasn't authorized to speak publicly.
Earlier this month, lawyers for Musk threatened to file a defamation lawsuit over the film.
Musk would not sit for an interview with Gibney.
Instead, he used an AI-generated avatar of Musk as a stand-in.
Bobby Allen, NPR News.
OpenAI says it's AI models engaged with U.S. government websites without the company's knowledge.
It's the latest episode of artificial intelligence going rogue, doing things the company didn't ask it to do or know about.
The company says the AI model accessed publicly available information from the Census Bureau
and also copied information from the SEC, posting it on another website.
This comes as an independent AI lab says models appearing to come from OpenAI also tricked,
tried to hack the Education Department, but were unsuccessful.
You're listening to NPR News.
